passages.t: A limit on punishment, and the ox that threshes
passages.happening:
When two men have a dispute, they are to go to court, ‘so that the innocent may be acquitted and the guilty condemned’ (verse 1).

If the guilty man is sentenced to a beating, it is to be given in the judge's presence, with a number of strokes that fits the wrong (verse 2). And there is a ceiling. “He may receive no more than forty lashes, lest your brother be beaten any more than that and be degraded in your sight” (verse 3).

Then a single line about an animal. “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
The laws of this chapter look unrelated. They share a concern for fairness and for dignity.

The first law puts three limits on punishment. It must follow a hearing. The judge must be present while it is carried out, so that it cannot turn into something worse behind his back. And it may never pass forty strokes, however serious the offense.

The reason given is the heart of the law. The guilty man is still called ‘your brother’. He has done wrong and he is punished. But he is not to be ‘degraded’. Punishment in Israel was to stop short of destroying a person's standing as a human being and a member of the people. A court may correct a man. It may not make him into a thing.

Later Jewish practice gave forty lashes less one, which kept safely under the limit. The apostle Paul received that punishment five times from synagogue courts, as a Jew under their discipline.

The ox. Grain was threshed by driving oxen round and round over the cut stalks on a hard floor. A muzzle stopped the animal from eating as it worked. The law forbids the muzzle. The ox that does the work may share in it.

It is a small law, and it shows how far the kindness of the law reaches. It reaches from the convicted man to the working animal.
passages.later:
Paul writes of his own experience of verse 3: “Five times I received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one” (2 Corinthians 11:24). The note on that verse explains that it is no charge against the Jewish people.

Paul quotes verse 4 twice, to say that those who work for the gospel should be supported by it. “For it is written in the Law of Moses: ‘Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.’ Is it about oxen that God is concerned?” (1 Corinthians 9:9). Interpreters differ on whether Paul means that the law was never about oxen, or that its principle of fair reward for work reaches beyond them.
passages.asks: Even the guilty man is ‘your brother’, and his punishment has a limit. Ask how you treat a person who has wronged you once the wrong has been dealt with, and whether you let them have their dignity back. And think of the ox. Ask whether those who work for you, or serve you, share fairly in what their work produces.

passages.t: A brother's duty to the dead
passages.happening:
Brothers live together, and one dies leaving no son. His widow is not to marry outside the family. “Her husband’s brother is to take her as his wife and fulfill the duty of a brother-in-law for her” (verse 5). The first son born will carry the dead man's name, ‘so that his name will not be blotted out from Israel’ (verse 6).

If the brother refuses, the widow may go to the elders at the gate and say so (verse 7). The elders speak with him. If he still says, ‘I do not want to marry her’, she is to take off his sandal in front of the elders, spit in his face, and say, ‘This is what is done to the man who will not maintain his brother’s line’ (verses 8-9).

His family is then known in Israel as ‘The House of the Unsandaled’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
This custom is called levirate marriage, from the Latin word for a brother-in-law. Customs like it are known from other law collections of the ancient world.

In Israel a man's name and his family's claim to its land passed through his sons. A man who died without a son was in danger of having his name die with him and his land pass to another line. His widow was left with no one to support her.

The duty of the brother answered both needs. The widow was kept within the family and provided for. The first son would count as the dead man's heir and take his share of land.

The law speaks of it as a duty. The Hebrew words are technical terms. This is not a love story. It is something a man does for his dead brother.

A brother who refused was, in effect, keeping his brother's share for himself. The law does not force him. What it does is give the widow a voice. She may take him to court. She speaks at the gate before the elders, and the last word in the scene is hers.

The sandal was connected with the right to walk on land and claim it. To take it off him was to show that he had given up his claim. The spitting and the nickname are public shame. In a small town that was a real penalty.

A modern reader will notice that the law does not ask what the widow herself would choose. It belongs to a world in which marriages were arranged by families and a woman alone had no means of living. Within that world it protects her and gives her standing to accuse a man who fails her. It is a law of ancient Israel and is not a rule for anyone's marriage today.
passages.later:
Genesis tells the oldest story of this duty. Judah said to his son Onan, “Sleep with your brother’s wife. Perform your duty as her brother-in-law and raise up offspring for your brother” (Genesis 38:8). Onan would not, and the widow, Tamar, was wronged before she was vindicated.

The book of Ruth shows a custom close to this one. Boaz says he has taken Ruth as his wife ‘to raise up the name of the deceased through his inheritance’ (Ruth 4:10), and a sandal is handed over at the gate (Ruth 4:7).

Tamar and Ruth are both named in Matthew's list of the ancestors of Jesus (Matthew 1:3, 5).

Some Sadducees put a question to Jesus based on this law. He answered, “In the resurrection, people will neither marry nor be given in marriage” (Matthew 22:30).
passages.asks: The brother was asked to spend himself for a name that was not his and a child who would not count as his own. Ask what you owe to people who can no longer repay you or even thank you. And notice that the law gave a widow the right to speak against a powerful relative in public. Ask who around you has a just complaint and no one to hear it.

passages.t: A severe penalty, and honest weights
passages.happening:
Verses 11 and 12 give a single case. Two men are fighting. The wife of one, to rescue her husband, seizes the other man by the genitals. The law says, “you are to cut off her hand. You must show her no pity.”

Then a law about trade. “You shall not have two differing weights in your bag, one heavy and one light. You shall not have two differing measures in your house, one large and one small” (verses 13-14). Weights and measures must be ‘accurate and honest’ (verse 15). “For everyone who behaves dishonestly in regard to these things is detestable to the LORD your God” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The first case is taken up in the hard question below.

The law of weights speaks to the market. In the ancient world a weight was a shaped stone carried in a bag. The Hebrew of verse 13 says, word for word, a stone and a stone, a large one and a small one. A merchant could use the heavy stone when he bought and the light stone when he sold, and so cheat every customer twice. Measures were containers, used in the same way for grain.

It was an easy fraud and hard to catch. It fell most heavily on the poor, who bought in small amounts and could not check.

Notice the word the law uses of it. Dishonest dealing is ‘detestable to the LORD’. That is the word this book uses for idols. God cares what is in the merchant's bag as he cares what is on the altar.

The promise attached is long life in the land. A people that cannot trust its own scales cannot live together.
passages.later:
The prophet Amos heard merchants planning exactly this: “Let us reduce the ephah and increase the shekel; let us cheat with dishonest scales” (Amos 8:5).

The book of Proverbs repeats the verdict: “Dishonest scales are an abomination to the LORD, but an accurate weight is His delight” (Proverbs 11:1).
passages.hard:
Why does the law say that the woman's hand must be cut off?

This is the only penalty of its kind in Israel's law apart from the formula ‘eye for eye’, and it jars. Its harshness should be admitted and not explained away.

Interpreters make two observations. The first is about the offense. It threatened the man's power to have children, and in Israel that meant the survival of his name, which is the concern of the law just before this one.

The second is about how the penalty was understood. Some Jewish interpreters in the time of the rabbis read it as a payment for the shame caused and not as the actual loss of a hand, in the same way that they read ‘eye for eye’ as payment. Others take it as written, a severe penalty meant to deter.

These notes do not settle it. This was a law of ancient Israel's courts. It is not given to the church, and no one may use it to justify harming any person.
passages.asks: A merchant with two sets of weights is one person when he buys and another when he sells. Ask whether you measure others by one standard and yourself by another. And ask whether you would be content for God to look into your accounts as he looks at your worship.

passages.happening:
The chapter closes with a memory and a command.

“Remember what the Amalekites did to you along your way from Egypt” (verse 17). They met Israel when it was ‘tired and weary’ and attacked the stragglers at the rear; ‘they had no fear of God’ (verse 18).

When Israel has rest in the land, it is to ‘blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven’. “Do not forget!” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The Amalekites were a wandering people of the southern desert. Exodus 17 tells how they attacked Israel soon after it left Egypt. Deuteronomy adds one detail: they struck the weary people at the back of the line.

That detail is the charge. The people at the rear of a marching column are the weak: the old, the sick, the exhausted, and those with small children. Amalek went for them. The text says they did it because ‘they had no fear of God’. In this book the fear of God is what holds a person back from harming those who cannot defend themselves.

The command to blot out Amalek is hard, and it belongs with the conquest texts. The hard question below takes it up.

The passage is built on two words, remember and blot out. Its last words in Hebrew are a sharp command two words long: do not forget.

Jewish tradition has often read the command to remember Amalek as a charge to resist cruelty toward the defenseless in every generation.
passages.later:
Exodus tells the first attack and God's word about it: “I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven” (Exodus 17:14).

King Saul was later sent against Amalek, and the story of how he carried it out is one of the hard pages of 1 Samuel (chapter 15).

In the book of Esther, the man who plots to destroy all the Jews of the Persian empire is called ‘Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite’ (Esther 3:1). Agag was the name of Amalek's king, and many readers, Jewish and Christian, have seen a deliberate link.
passages.hard:
How should the command to blot out Amalek be read?

A reader who is troubled by the conquest texts will be troubled by this one, and should be.

The text presents the command as judgment on a people who attacked the weak with no fear of God, and the Old Testament shows Amalek as an attacker more than once. The ways Christians read the conquest commands, set out in the note on chapter 7, verses 1 to 5, and in the note on chapter 20, apply here too. Some read the command as God's judgment at one point in history. Some read its language as the sweeping idiom of ancient war. Some read it as a stage in God's making himself known, to be read in the light of Christ. Each has a cost, and these notes take no side.

Christians have generally read the command as one that belonged to Israel's own history and is not a pattern for today. Jewish tradition has often read it as a call to oppose cruelty to the defenseless.

One thing must be said plainly. No people living today is Amalek. No one may use this passage to justify violence or contempt toward any person or people, and it has no nation or conflict of today in view.
passages.asks: Amalek's sin was to go after the weakest at the back of the line. Ask who is at the back of the line where you live and work, and how they are treated. And ask what the fear of God holds you back from doing when no one could stop you.
